title: [15/2/2025] Employees and factories producing silk in England and Wales

frame.name: Introduction
paragraphs: The table illustrates the changes, by decade, in the number of male and female workers in the silk industry of England and Wales, along with the number of factories, from 1851 to 1901.

frame.name: Overview
paragraphs: Overall, despite the fact that the silk industry underwent a consistent reduction in the workforce across both genders, there was an initial boom in the number of factories, followed by a slight decline over time. In addition, the sector maintained higher female representation throughout the period, with women consistently outnumbering men.

frame.name: Body 1
paragraphs: With regard to the labour force, in 1851, employment was at its highest level, at nearly 131,000 people, comprising roughly 54,000 males and 77,000 females. Over the surveyed period, the total workforce in this sector significantly declined, falling to just under 39,000 workers by 1901, roughly a third of the initial figure. The decline affected both genders, with female employment levels decreasing sharply to just over 25,000 in the final year, while males’ figures had fallen more dramatically to 13,000 by 1901, despite experiencing a slight recovery in 1891.

frame.name: Body 2
paragraphs: In terms of factory numbers, there were only 272 silk-processing facilities at the start of the period. However, in the next decade, the number of production sites tripled, reaching a peak of 761 locations in 1861, before gradually declining over the following four decades to 623 by 1901.
